title: POC scoping - SDK adapter & structured output - Horizon Transport
summary: Discovery and POC scoping for a 6-week pilot: integrate Redwood via an SDK adapter to hit 100 tps inference for short-response ETA/dispatch assistant; define success criteria (latency p95 < 120ms for 64 token responses, cost target, structured JSON output validation), benchmark plan, timeline, and SSO/KMS requirements. Agreed next step: Redwood to send POC SOW and benchmark template; customer to provide sample workload and schema by 2025-06-02.
topics: Integration approach: SDK adapter vs OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Function/tool calling and structured output validation
next_steps: Redwood to send draft POC SOW (workload profile + benchmark plan) by 2025-06-02
Horizon to share sample payloads, JSON schema, and production traffic histogram by 2025-06-02
Schedule 60-min technical setup call (SE + Horizon infra) for 2025-06-05
Redwood to provide preliminary cost estimate for 6-week pilot and recommended model/quantization profiles by 2025-06-04
action_items: Maya Chen: Draft and send POC SOW and benchmark spreadsheet (due 2025-06-02)
Diego Ramos: Prepare initial benchmark harness and sample client adapter code (due 2025-06-04)
Laura Kim: Share representative message traces, JSON schemas, and peak/minute traffic histogram (due 2025-06-02)
Owen Patel: Confirm VPC peering and KMS requirements and share firewall/IP allowlist window (due 2025-06-06)
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-05-29, Start: 15:00 UTC, Duration: ~52 mins. Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Laura (Horizon - Head of AI), Owen (Horizon - SRE), Samir (Horizon - PM).

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros and then we can dive into the POC scope.
[00:07] Laura (Horizon): Hi, Laura here. We're excited to see the integration options. Our main use case is an operational assistant for dispatch and ETA predictions, short responses but very high qps at peaks.
[00:18] Samir (Horizon): Samir here — product owner. Key outcomes: accurate structured output (JSON with specific fields), maintain sub-200ms latencies, and keep inference costs predictable.
[00:28] Diego (Redwood SE): Thanks. Diego from Redwood, I focus on latency/benchmarks. Can you give the rough traffic profile? QPS, typical token lengths?
[00:36] Laura (Horizon): Peak bursts up to ~3k reqs/minute for the dispatcher service, so about 50 rps sustained with spikes to 100 rps; most responses are short, 30-80 tokens. We also have a lower-priority batch scoring job that can be async.
[00:52] Owen (Horizon): From infra side, we need VPC peering or private connectivity, SSO via Okta, and key management in our KMS. Also strict audit logs for each request.
[01:05] Maya: Great context. Our typical POC pattern — we size a small dedicated pool or run hosted with reserved throughput depending on SLOs. For this profile, we usually recommend starting with a dedicated instance pool to hit consistent p95 latency.
[01:20] Samir: Cost is important — can you ballpark cost per 10k requests for short prompts?
[01:25] Diego: We'll give a more precise estimate once we know batching parameters and model choice. For a 64-token reply target, on optimized open models with quantization we often hit 0.4–0.7 cents per request at scale but depends on batching and caching. That's a rough range.
[01:40] Laura: That range is helpful. Our acceptance criteria: 95th percentile latency under 120ms for the live endpoint, structured JSON validated against schema with >98% success, and cost below X (we'll finalise when you share estimate).
[01:52] Diego: Noted. Let's define the benchmark metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, tokens/cost, success rate for JSON schema validation, and throughput at target concurrency. We'll run automated replay of traces.
[02:07] Samir: For schema validation, we need strict keys: {eta_seconds, confidence, confidence_reasons[], update_required:boolean}. We expect predictable ordering and consistent types.
[02:18] Maya: On structured output — Redwood supports tool/function calling and structured output enforcement via a schema-check step. For POC, we can wire function-calling or use structured output mode and run an automated validator in the harness.
[02:35] Laura: We prefer function-calling because we want deterministic fields and integrated downstream processing. Can Redwood's adapter guarantee a fallback if the model emits free text?
[02:44] Diego: Yes — we implement a post-processing validator. If model output fails schema, there are fallback policies: deterministic retry with stronger system prompt, invoke function call with stricter signature, or route to a slower but more precise variant (e.g., non-quantized model). We can measure the failure rate in the benchmark.
[02:59] Owen: On connectivity, can you support OpenAI-compatible endpoints? Our platform already has an OpenAI-style client and we'd prefer not to rewrite everything.
[03:09] Maya: Redwood offers both an SDK adapter and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. The adapter is small — typically a single file client shim — and supports function calls/structured-output helpers. The OpenAI-compatible path is easiest: minimal change for your engineers.
[03:22] Laura: Good. Any tradeoffs between adapter vs OpenAI endpoints?
[03:26] Diego: Adapter gives more control: built-in batching logic, smarter retry hooks, and direct hooks for prefix/KV caching you might want for conversational state. The OpenAI-compatible endpoint is quickest to ship but you may lose some advanced batching/caching unless you implement client-side batching. Performance differences are small if you use Redwood's SDK which does continuous batching.
[03:46] Samir: We also use an internal gateway that aggregates calls; we might prefer the adapter at the gateway layer.
[03:52] Maya: That maps well — you can run the adapter inside the gateway, letting it surface metrics and manage batching. We'll provide sample adapter code for Node and Go.
[04:02] Owen: For benchmarks, how do you replay traces — do you preserve inter-arrival times and concurrency?
[04:07] Diego: Yes—we replay with a trace-preserving harness, configurable arrival distributions, and can inject larger spikes. We'll run multiple model variants: standard FP16, 4-bit quant, and a conservative full-precision run to measure best-case quality.
[04:20] Laura: For the benchmark outputs, we need to see request/response IDs mapped back to original traces and the schema validation failure hits so we can triage.
[04:29] Diego: We'll include per-request diagnostics, token-level cost, and per-route latency histograms. We'll also bucket by prompt length and by concurrency.
[04:38] Samir: Timeline question — we want a 6-week pilot, start-first-integration by mid-June. Is that doable?
[04:44] Maya: Yes, 6-week pilot is our standard. Proposed schedule: Week 0 (setup + sample artifacts), Week 1 (bench harness + initial run), Week 2-3 (iterative tuning and schema robustness tests), Week 4 (user-simulated stress tests), Week 5 (report + tweaks), Week 6 (handoff + recommendations).
[04:58] Owen: For security, we need SOC2 boundary info, per-request audit logs, and KMS key handling — can Redwood bind to our KMS and keep keys in customer-managed KMS?
[05:09] Maya: Yes — for private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and can enable audit logs. For hosted POC we can do encrypted-in-transit and at-rest with Redwood-managed keys, but for Horizon's requirements we'd likely run a private deployment or dedicated capacity with KMS integration.
[05:22] Laura: We also care about data retention: we must not keep any payloads beyond 30 days and we need an automated purge.
[05:29] Diego: That's configurable at route-level retention. We'll document retention policy in the SOW.
[05:35] Samir: Any blockers on our side? We need to provide sample payloads and network contacts. Owen will handle infra.
[05:41] Owen: I'll prepare the allowlist, provide KMS requirements, and confirm whether we prefer VPC peering or private link.
[05:47] Maya: Great. Quick recap: Redwood will send a POC SOW + benchmark template by 2025-06-02; Horizon shares payloads and traffic histograms by the same date; then we set up the technical kickoff on 2025-06-05. Primary success criteria reiterated: p95 < 120ms, JSON schema pass rate >98%, cost within target.
[06:06] Laura: Sounds good. Also please include a short appendix in the SOW describing fallback policies and function-calling guarantees.
[06:14] Diego: We'll include fallback matrix: retry rules, alternate model variants, and how we degrade gracefully (e.g., drop to cached answer or route to async scoring).
[06:25] Samir: One more question: do you support streaming for partial updates? We sometimes need progressive ETA updates.
[06:31] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports streaming responses and partial outputs; for structured streaming we can emit partial JSON chunks or a delta function call pattern — we'll advise on the most robust approach in the SOW.
[06:43] Laura: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[06:46] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up.

Notes: transcript contains some minor mishears and filler words; speaker tags approximate. End of transcript.
